{"id": "6:153/q14", "question": "What does the bāʾ in 'fa-tafarraqa bikum' do?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition directly marks caused scattering or accompaniment that implies causation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q14/p1", "position": "It is causative: the paths divide and scatter you.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn allows an object-like semantic role; al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī say the bāʾ makes the paths the agent, stronger than saying travelers divide themselves."}, {"id": "6:153/q14/p2", "position": "It marks accompaniment: you diverge together with the paths.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports a circumstantial reading; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares dhahabtu bi-Zayd with adhhabtuhu, so figurative accompaniment yields a causative force."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q15", "question": "What is the result of following divergent paths?", "turns_on": "The phrase can be glossed as departure from religion, disruption of unity, and its ultimate destination.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q15/p1", "position": "They cause deviation from God's religion and shatter religious unity.", "reasons": "Mujāhid glosses deviation and opposition; al-Māwardī adds loss of unity in defending religion; al-Ṭabrisī calls it God's chosen religion. Al-Qurṭubī cites 6:159; Ibn Kathīr cites 42:13 and earlier peoples' disputes; Elmalılı says factionalism weakens those who abandon tawḥīd."}, {"id": "6:153/q15/p2", "position": "Side roads lead ultimately to Hell, while the one path leads to Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's road image and Qatāda's report give the contrasted destinations; al-Bursawī connects deviation here to slipping from the afterlife bridge and cites a report on many who slip."}, {"id": "6:153/q15/p3", "position": "The word literally means becoming scattered.", "reasons": "Asad gives this literal rendering."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q16", "question": "To whom does the pronoun in 'His path' refer?", "turns_on": "The antecedent is God, but the literary account depends on who says 'My path'.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q16/p1", "position": "To God; the phrase denotes His religion or Islam.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the context determines the referent, and if 'My path' is divine, the third person is iltifāt. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī locates the person shift here even when 'My path' belongs to Muhammad."}, {"id": "6:153/q16/p2", "position": "It may follow the Prophet's quotation of God's command or a new divine address.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses these alternatives to account for the switch after a prophet-owned 'My path'."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q17", "question": "What does 'that is what He charged you with' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative gathers the immediate final injunction or the wider revelation and preceding ordinances.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q17/p1", "position": "The comprehensive charge to follow the one path and avoid divergent paths.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the closing repeats both commands; al-Bursawī counts this as the tenth duty; al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the threefold repeated testament, each closing a group of duties."}, {"id": "6:153/q17/p2", "position": "The Qurʾān, Islam, previous commands, avoidance of sin, or obedience that averts punishment.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits this range without selecting one."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q18", "question": "What is the standing of these commandments across scriptures and peoples?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over the exact Torah formulation, while the universal and unabrogated status is repeatedly asserted.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q18/p1", "position": "They are decisive, universal, and never abrogated in any revealed book.", "reasons": "Muqātil extends them to all Adam's descendants; Ibn ʿAbbās calls them Mother of the Book. Several reports promise Paradise for practice and Hell for abandonment; Elmalılı distinguishes enduring fundamentals from rulings that vary by time and place. Al-Bursawī counts ten duties; Iṭqān notes three clear verses beginning at 6:151, with another three at 17:23."}, {"id": "6:153/q18/p2", "position": "They were the Torah's first instruction or first ten verses.", "reasons": "Kaʿb swears to the Torah priority; some reports say first thing, others first ten verses. Al-Kashshāf and al-Ṭabrisī name the opening 'Say: come...' as the Torah start."}, {"id": "6:153/q18/p3", "position": "The next verse's gift of Moses' Book links these commands to all prophetic communities.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī coordinates 'Then We gave Moses the Book' with 'He charged you,' making this an ancient command passed through each prophet."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q19", "question": "What reports associate these three verses with the Prophet's testament or pledge?", "turns_on": "Different reports attach the verses to a sealed testament, a pledge, or a missionary encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q19/p1", "position": "They are the Prophet's sealed testament, to be recited from 6:151 through 6:153.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's report is graded ḥasan gharīb by al-Tirmidhī and ḥasan by al-Ālūsī. Al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym recites or writes these verses when asked for a sealed sheet or advice."}, {"id": "6:153/q19/p2", "position": "The Prophet sought a pledge on the three verses, promising reward for fulfillment and leaving unpunished breaches to God's will.", "reasons": "ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit reports that worldly punishment expiates a breach, while God may punish or pardon a deferred one."}, {"id": "6:153/q19/p3", "position": "At Minā the Prophet recited these commands to an Arab tribe after inviting them to monotheism, his mission, and his protection.", "reasons": "The Durr report says he then recited 16:90; Mafrūq praised the morals and Hāniʾ approved the words."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q20", "question": "What does the closing hope for taqwā mean?", "turns_on": "The sources dispute how the three endings relate to each duty group and whether the final aim primarily stresses following or avoiding division.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q20/p1", "position": "Obey God and fear His punishment by keeping His commands and avoiding prohibitions.", "reasons": "Mujāhid glosses mindfulness as obedience; ʿAṭāʾ as fear. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk mentions the five prayers guarding against Hell. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say the complete way protects from the Fire and brings lasting salvation. Al-Itqān explains the closing purpose as guarding against God's punishment for abandoning His religious law."}, {"id": "6:153/q20/p2", "position": "Taqwā comes from adhering to the one path and refusing divisive alternatives.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses avoidance of division as the verse's main purpose; he objects to Abū Ḥayyān's priority on following the path. He links piety to human nature in 91:7–8, while Iṣlāḥī says divine reminder awakens nature."}, {"id": "6:153/q20/p3", "position": "The endings progress from reason through remembrance to piety.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says obvious prior prohibitions call for reason and later desire-related ones for recollection; al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Iṣlāḥī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describe reflection leading to heed and precaution. Al-Ṭabrisī notes the neighboring tadhakkarūn readings with light or doubled consonant, from tatadhakkarūn by deletion or assimilation."}, {"id": "6:153/q20/p4", "position": "The first duties are obvious, while the second group is harder to delimit.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts five obvious duties with four requiring thought; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the claim of obscurity, allowing only care over orphan property and measures."}, {"id": "6:153/q20/p5", "position": "The first ending addresses idolaters' ignorance and the second their remembered virtues.", "reasons": "Al-Quṭb al-Rāzī is quoted through Rūḥ al-Maʿānī; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects it as historically inaccurate and confusing Qurʾānic recollection with ordinary memory."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q21", "question": "How does the verse connect with its neighboring verses and the sūra?", "turns_on": "The sources connect the command to the three-verse sequence, Abrahamic and Qurʾānic guidance, and later anti-division warnings.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q21/p1", "position": "It gathers the preceding commands and prepares the renewed warning against religious division.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says prohibitions and orders culminate in the one-way command; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates 42:13 and treats the path declaration as prelude to the warning. Ibn ʿĀshūr finds three linked sections: social order, economic relations, and Islam's inclusive principle. Al-Biqāʿī compares 6:126 and the three testament endings."}, {"id": "6:153/q21/p2", "position": "It restates Abraham's religion against Quraysh's invented practices and prepares the surah's closing proclamation.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī traces the passage from Quraysh's invented food taboos through Abraham's duties to 6:155–165; he says Moses' law guided Israelites on the same path and a demanded sign cannot replace prophetic guidance. Kur'an Yolu contrasts baseless polytheist rules with nine duties and the encompassing tenth."}, {"id": "6:153/q21/p3", "position": "It connects to warnings against sitting with disputants and against sectarian division.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites 6:68 and 4:140 for avoiding disputants and 6:159 for religious fragmentation; Ibn Kathīr links 42:13, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise invokes prophetic unity."}, {"id": "6:153/q21/p4", "position": "The Qurʾān's revealed authority and universal prophetic mission underpin the call.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says messengers remove excuses (4:165), Muhammad is the final universal messenger to humans and jinn (7:158; 6:19), and all reached by the Qurʾān are warned. He cites 11:17 and 68:44–45 on rejection, the 'red and black' report explained by Mujāhid, 41:42 on revelation's integrity, 4:82, 38:29 and 47:24 on reflection, and 3:187 and 3:77 against concealment."}, {"id": "6:153/q21/p5", "position": "The sūra's final verses invite choice while making each person accountable.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says people ma

{"id": "6:153/q22", "question": "Where were these three verses revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q22/p1", "position": "They are an exception revealed in Medina within an otherwise Meccan sūra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Shahr b. Al-Burhān says reports establish that al-Anʿām is Meccan apart from six verses, including the closing passage beginning 'Say: Come'."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q23", "question": "What response to religious innovations is drawn from the warning?", "turns_on": "The reports range from counsel to preserve Sunnah through social and legal sanctions to severe eschatological warnings.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q23/p1", "position": "Follow transmitted Sunnah and avoid innovations, excessive dispute and sectarian desires.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites Ibn Masʿūd's rebuke of pebble-counting devotional circles: good intent does not validate an act. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz advises simple inherited religion; Abū al-ʿĀliya urges the original practice, which al-Ḥasan confirms. Sahl says public disputation spread innovation; Ibn Masʿūd warns against hair-splitting. Al-Tustarī cites a severe no-repentance saying."}, {"id": "6:153/q23/p2", "position": "Persistent company with innovators shares their judgment; avoid sitting with them even to dispute.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites 6:68 and 4:140 and attributes the rule to Aḥmad, al-Awzāʿī and Ibn al-Mubārak; he compares ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's treatment of companions of drinkers."}, {"id": "6:153/q23/p3", "position": "Innovation can block repentance or Paradise and is spiritually worse than an ordinary sin.", "reasons": "Tustarī's attributed report says repentance is narrowed or barred for innovations. Sahl cites a report barring innovators from Paradise; Sufyān calls innovation dearer to Iblīs since its followers do not repent; al-Awzāʿī relates Iblīs's strategy. Al-Fuḍayl warns that love of an innovator harms deeds and heart."}, {"id": "6:153/q23/p4", "position": "Some sectarian doctrines and conduct are treated especially severely.", "reasons": "Sahl rejects prayer behind or marriage with the Muʿtazila and lists their disputed doctrines; al-Shaʿbī gives a fiery etymology of people of desires. Al-Qurṭubī recalls 72/73 sect reports, a proposed extra anti-scholar sect, and Rāfiʿ's warning about people equating Iblīs with God in creative power."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q24", "question": "What is the rhetorical force of the repeated testament and appeal to piety?", "turns_on": "The rhetorical emphasis may fall on comprehensive obedience or on the closing anti-division warning.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q24/p1", "position": "The three repeated charges strengthen acceptance, with reason, recollection and piety marking a progression.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī stresses the three verse endings; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls them linked sections, and al-Nasafī and Iṣlāḥī explain the mental sequence. Al-Ālūsī says the comprehensive path warrants emphatic repetition."}, {"id": "6:153/q24/p2", "position": "The path declaration leads to the prohibition on division, which explains the final piety clause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts this discourse focus with Abū Ḥayyān's emphasis on following the comprehensive path."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q25", "question": "What other word-choice and simile observations are cited alongside these notes?", "turns_on": "The cited material ranges from composite image syntax to other terms for travel and number choice.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q25/p1", "position": "A composite simile makes a combined scene a single image, while independent similes remain separate.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī contrasts Bashshār's dust and flashing swords with separate comparisons; Ruʾba's markings and al-Buḥturī's horse and cloud also depend on combined appearance. He argues Bashshār's conjunction keeps the image attached, compares wa with maʿa, and cites the undivided she-camel and calf conditional."}, {"id": "6:153/q25/p2", "position": "Sulūk can mean traveling along a path, broader than merely entering.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts Moses' usluk in Qasas, with its repeated journeys from the chest to Midian and back, with adkhil in Naml, where dakhal forms occur five times and the story opens at the fire; he cites 27:7, 27:12, 28:7, 28:11, 28:22, 28:29, 28:32 and 71:19–20."}, {"id": "6:153/q25/p3", "position": "Other singular and plural choices follow distinct semantic or phonological patterns.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān says Hell is singular as one substance but Paradise may be many gardens; al-albāb occurs only in plural because its singular is heavy; east and west vary among singular direction, dual seasonal points and plural numerous points."}]}

{"id": "6:31/q01", "question": "Who are the people declared losers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q01/p1", "position": "Deniers of resurrection and the afterlife, especially the previously mentioned worldly life claimants; Quraysh and their followers are included.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies resurrection, judgment, Paradise and Hell. {"id": "6:31/q02", "question": "What reports identify a particular denier or occasion for this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports name different people or give different statements.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q02/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl acknowledged Muhammad's truth but refused to follow a man from Banū ʿAbd Manāf.", "reasons": "Abū Yazīd al-Madanī reports a handshake and this statement before the verse was revealed."}, {"id": "6:31/q02/p2", "position": "Abū Jahl said he did not call Muhammad a liar but rejected the message.", "reasons": "Nājiya ibn Kaʿb reports the verse followed this admission."}, {"id": "6:31/q02/p3", "position": "Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir privately believed Muhammad truthful but feared Arab retaliation and loss of safety if he followed him.", "reasons": "Maqātil identifies him."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q03", "question": "What loss have the deniers incurred, and why?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is explained as the failed faith transaction, squandered human capacities, or the word's basic lexical sense.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q03/p1", "position": "They forfeit afterlife reward and gain punishment by exchanging faith for unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī likens faith and Paradise to the capital of a ruined transaction; Wāḥidī's authorities say the worst loss is one's soul, like losing a merchant's capital; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies afterlife rather than worldly deprivation. Al-Rāzī counts lost reward and incurred punishment as two losses. Biqāʿī says every attainable reward is lost; Bayḍāwī adds lost blessing and enduring punishment; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it a failed bargain."}, {"id": "6:31/q03/p2", "position": "They squander faculties meant for lasting knowledge and virtue on passing pleasure, and lack provisions for the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī names bodily and intellectual faculties as capital, transient pleasure as imagined profit, and alienation after death from both spiritual preparation and worldly attachments; Biqāʿī adds outer senses, reason and prophetic miracles. Study Quran relays Rāzī's investment analogy."}, {"id": "6:31/q03/p3", "position": "Loss fundamentally means decrease, though some derive it from destruction.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports both derivations."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q04", "question": "What does 'meeting God' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether meeting is understood as resurrection and recompense, an implied object such as reward, literal vision, or a representational encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q04/p1", "position": "Resurrection, return to God, and His judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās includes reward and punishment and cites 2:46; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes God's power and the consequences of deeds; Rāzī says benefit and harm then lie with God alone. Kashshāf likens standing before the Lord to a guilty servant detained and rebuked. Qaffāl cites the warning concerning a false oath for property. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes the passage's progression from resurrection and gathering to meeting."}, {"id": "6:31/q04/p2", "position": "Meeting God's promised reward and punishment, or the recompense of one's deeds, is figuratively called meeting God.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī cites ordinary speech about a dead person meeting his deeds; Ṭabrisī attributes the promise gloss to Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan; al-Ālūsī notes an implicit complement and possessive magnification in Abū Ḥayyān."}, {"id": "6:31/q04/p3", "position": "The phrase retains actual meeting or vision of God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī rejects extending contextual figurative uses to this verse and argues denial of God and His vision implies denial of existence; Nasafī notes denying resurrection also denies vision. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects ending loss because its deprivation occurs at resurrection and not all deniers lose worldly goods."}, {"id": "6:31/q05/p2", "position": "The ordinary loss lasts until Judgment, when a worse calamity eclipses it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī analogizes Satan's curse 'until Judgment' at 38:78. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports and rejects commentators who end the loss there."}, {"id": "6:31/q05/p3", "position": "Before 'when', ḥattā is initial and indicates cause rather than an endpoint.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Ḥājib says the sense is effectively 'when the Hour comes'."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q06", "question": "What event is 'the Hour' here?", "turns_on": "Whether the lament and burden occur at actual resurrection, its onset, or death.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q06/p1", "position": "The resurrection, gathering and universal judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies raising the dead from graves; Abū Ḥayyān argues simultaneous bearing of burdens better fits actual resurrection and says those in barzakh experience its interval as a day. {"id": "6:31/q07", "question": "Why is it called 'the Hour'?", "turns_on": "The proposed relation of the name to speed, sudden onset, brevity, or fame.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q07/p1", "position": "Reckoning and recompense occur swiftly.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī, Samīn and Elmalılı explain the name through rapid accounting; al-Ālūsī says sāʿa first denotes a short interval."}, {"id": "6:31/q07/p2", "position": "It arrives at an unexpected, unknown instant.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī prefers sudden onset because baghtatan follows; Elmalılı says only God knows its hour."}, {"id": "6:31/q07/p3", "position": "Its duration is brief compared with eternity.", "reasons": "Nasafī compares the intervening interval with the eternal sequel; al-Ālūsī also reports this."}, {"id": "6:31/q07/p4", "position": "The definite article identifies the known, uniquely famous Hour.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is established in minds and implied by meeting God; Samīn compares 'the star' and al-Thurayyā. Al-Ṭabarī calls it the known Hour."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q08", "question": "What does 'suddenly' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q08/p1", "position": "An unforeseen onset without knowing its time or receiving warning.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites Arab usage and a poem of unforeseen death; Ibn ʿAbbās says God alone knows the Hour; Samīn stresses mere speed of an expected event is insufficient and cites poetry. {"id": "6:31/q09", "question": "How is 'baghtatan' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative describes a state or supplies/emphasizes a verbal action.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q09/p1", "position": "An accusative circumstantial verbal noun describing the Hour or those it overtakes.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya cite Sībawayh's nonproductive parallel qataltuhu ṣabran; Naḥḥās adds a poetic laʾyan bi-laʾy. {"id": "6:31/q10", "question": "What reports describe the Hour's arrival?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different preceding circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q10/p1", "position": "It can arrive while someone eats or two people trade, leaving their acts unfinished.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits the Prophetic report through Abū Hurayra."}, {"id": "6:31/q10/p2", "position": "A caller will announce the Hour three times before it arrives.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports ʿIkrima."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q11", "question": "How does 'jāʾa' here relate to Qur'anic use of 'atā'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q11/p1", "position": "Its force depends on the full verse and context; the supplied comparison is not completed.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the Hour here and 6:40–41; his other discussion describes Ghāfir 40:82–85, where peoples mocked messengers and believed only after seeing punishment, too late to help. He cautions against isolating either verb. Al-Sāmarrāʾī completes the comparison: jāʾa suits the deniers' harsher afterlife arrival, with regret and burdens, whereas atā suits a lighter worldly crisis in which God may remove the affliction (6:30–31, 6:40–41). He argues that jāʾa is heavier in sound and says the Qur'an uses only its past form, while atā appears in several conjugations; the heavier form matches the harsher scene."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q12", "question": "What does 'ḥasra' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q12/p1", "position": "Intense regret or grief for something lost.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as regret. Baghawī compares a traveler whose mount fails; al-Rāghib derives it from exposure or exhausted strength. Ṭabrisī says remorse exhausts the regretful."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q13", "question": "What does calling out to 'our regret' do?", "turns_on": "Whether the figurative address is described as summoning regret or alerting the hearers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q13/p1", "position": "It figuratively summons regret as if its appointed moment has arrived, magnifying anguish.", "reasons": "Sībawayh explains 'O wonder/regret, come'; Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Samīn and others say the abstraction cannot literally answer. Samīn adds rebuke for causing this need; Biqāʿī says the image warns others. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'our' fixes their own fate, unlike a bare cry often made for others; the following ʿalā marks the cause."}, {"id": "6:31/q13/p2", "position": "It alerts listeners to the terrible loss; the apparent addressee is the audience, not regret.", "reasons": "Zajjāj cites 'do not let me see you here' as an analogous displaced addressee; Sībawayh uses 'O wonder'; Wāḥidī cites 36:30, 39:56, 11:72 and 12:84. {"id": "6:31/q14", "question": "What are they lamenting?", "turns_on": "Whether their regret is specified as missed deeds, lost Paradise homes, mocked messengers, the failed bargain, or wasted faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q14/p1", "position": "Neglected faith, obedience and preparation for Paradise and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī specifies deeds that would earn Paradise; Muqātil names remembrance of God; Rāzī says lost reward, while their burdens indicate earned punishment. Biqāʿī includes disciplining the soul and following messengers; Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Study Quran specify afterlife work during worldly life."}, {"id": "6:31/q14/p2", "position": "They see the Paradise places they have lost and lament.", "reasons": "A Prophetic report is transmitted by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Qurṭubī, Ṭabrisī, Durr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī; Durr calls its chain sound. Samīn rejects the proposed pronoun reference to those places as remote; al-Ālūsī says the report cannot settle that reference."}, {"id": "6:31/q14/p3", "position": "They regret having mocked the messengers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Mujāhid."}, {"id": "6:31/q14/p4", "position": "They regret the ruined transaction of trading faith and Paradise for disbelief and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī infers the bargain from khusira; Qurṭubī cites 2:16."}, {"id": "6:31/q14/p5", "position": "They lament wasted capacities and separation from former pleasures.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says God-given faculties were meant to disclose enduring truth and virtue; after death they are unprepared for the spiritual realm and cut off from transient pleasures. {"id": "6:31/q16", "question": "What is the grammatical role of 'mā' in their lament?", "turns_on": "Whether mā names the act of neglect or the things neglected.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q16/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun: they lament their neglect.", "reasons": "Samīn says 'for what we neglected' attaches to regret."}, {"id": "6:31/q16/p2", "position": "It is a relative pronoun for deeds or acts of obedience they neglected.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī say on this analysis the antecedent is explicit in their speech; Abū Ḥayyān and Rāzī also report it."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q17", "question": "What does the pronoun in 'fīhā' refer to?", "turns_on": "Which implied antecedent—world, Hour, Paradise, bargain, deeds, or Paradise places—fits the context.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q17/p1", "position": "Worldly life, where they neglected work for the afterlife.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say the unmentioned world is obvious from context; Rāzī says reason identifies it as the place of neglect."}, {"id": "6:31/q17/p2", "position": "The Hour and the faith and preparation it required.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and others construe 'in it' as neglecting its affairs or preparation; Kashshāf compares 'I neglected God's side' at 39:56."}, {"id": "6:31/q17/p3", "position": "Paradise, which they failed to seek and work for.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī gives this reading and Ṭabrisī pairs it with the report of Hell's people seeing their Paradise homes. Al-Ālūsī considers it remote."}, {"id": "6:31/q17/p4", "position": "The transaction implied by their loss.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī argues loss implies sale, even without an explicit noun; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes the implied bargain. Samīn attributes it to al-Ḥasan."}, {"id": "6:31/q17/p5", "position": "The good deeds or acts of obedience expressed by a relative 'mā'.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Rāzī and al-Ālūsī note this makes the pronoun refer to an item in the utterance itself; Ibn al-Jawzī reports obedience as the antecedent."}, {"id": "6:31/q17/p6", "position": "Their former places in Paradise.", "reasons": "Samīn reports and rejects this proposal as remote."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q18", "question": "How does 'while they carry' attach to the lament?", "turns_on": "Whether the state is simultaneous with the cry or anticipated.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q18/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing them as they speak.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Samīn, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī identify the wāw as circumstantial; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say the explicit subject pronoun strengthens attribution."}, {"id": "6:31/q18/p2", "position": "The burden-bearing may be prospective relative to the lament.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī permits this alternate timing."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q19", "question": "What are 'their awzār'?", "turns_on": "Whether awzār names sins, their punishment, divine wrath, ignored reminders, or inward attachments.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q19/p1", "position": "Their sins, errors and evil deeds, described as heavy burdens.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites 94:2–3; Ibn ʿAbbās and many others gloss sin; Qatāda says the load is their deeds and also their work or earning. Ṭabarī rejects physical-load gloss as unattested Arab usage, preferring the sinning sense. Asad adopts Ibn ʿAbbās through Rāzī."}, {"id": "6:31/q19/p2", "position": "The punishment or suffering earned by their sins.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās records this as a second gloss; Zajjāj and others compare severe punishment to a crushing load, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes sin's consequence among possibilities."}, {"id": "6:31/q19/p3", "position": "God's wrath earned by sin.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 2:61, 2:90, 3:112 and 3:162."}, {"id": "6:31/q19/p4", "position": "The reminders and warnings they ignored.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 20:100–101, where the reminder becomes an afterlife burden."}, {"id": "6:31/q19/p5", "position": "For the veiled soul, attachments, bodily love, sins and sensory traits rooted within it.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says these bind, veil and torment the person."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q20", "question": "What is the root sense and derivation of 'wizr'?", "turns_on": "Whether the lexical starting point is carried weight or a refuge/support.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q20/p1", "position": "A heavy load; sins are named for the weight one carries.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites 94:2–3; Abū ʿUbayd describes carrying goods in a cloak and the loads of war. Wāḥidī cites 6:164; Samīn gives awzār as plural of wizr, war equipment and a poetic line, and wazīr as bearer of a ruler's burdens. Akhfash gives wazara/yaziru/wizran and mawzūr; Yūnus notes two vocalizations. Funeral usage prefers mawzūrāt over common maʾzūrāt, while Abū ʿAlī calls the latter sound-following."}, {"id": "6:31/q20/p2", "position": "A mountain refuge or support on which one relies; heaviness and support extend to sin and a minister.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Abū ʿUbayd cite Moses' request for Aaron as minister (20:29–30); Samīn and al-Rāghib cite 75:11. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls derivation from a refuge or helper unclear."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q21", "question": "How are their burdens borne 'on their backs'?", "turns_on": "Whether the image presents embodied deeds, metaphorical hardship, constant attachment, or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q21/p1", "position": "Literally: deeds take visible forms, and the sinner's ugly, foul deed rides or is carried on his back.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the deed demands to be carried; reports from al-Suddī, ʿAmr, Abū Marzūq and ʿUmayr include a grave-companion, a public exposure or a journey to Hell. Some describe the believer's fragrant good deed as a mount (19:85). Bursevī argues afterlife deeds can become visible though accidents here; al-Ālūsī sees no obstacle and cites Sunni belief in embodied deeds and weighing. Abū Ḥayyān's preferred report groups ʿUmayr, ʿAmr, al-Suddī and Ṭabarī."}, {"id": "6:31/q21/p2", "position": "Figuratively: sins and their painful punishment weigh on them like loads.", "reasons": "Zajjāj says Arabic uses 'heavy' for severe aversion; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats back-bearing as an intensified figure and questions the refuge derivation. Zamakhsharī compares hands as the normal instrument of deeds in 42:30; Bursevī calls sins bodily loads by metaphor."}, {"id": "6:31/q21/p3", "position": "The image says sins never leave or release them.", "reasons": "Arabists compare a person always before one's eyes to one continually in mind; Nasafī and Qurṭubī say sin clings to the denier."}, {"id": "6:31/q21/p4", "position": "Inwardly, rooted traits and attachments veil and torment the soul.", "reasons": "Qāshānī calls this the burden of bodily love and sensory traits."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q22", "question": "Why mention the backs specifically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q22/p1", "position": "The back is the customary and strongest place for heavy burdens, intensifying their weight.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī notes loads might otherwise be borne on head or shoulder; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say the back carries more, with Samīn comparing the hand's touch in 6:7. Kashshāf contrasts hand imagery for earned deeds in 42:30. Burhān also contrasts backs with heads: backs bear weight better."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q23", "question": "What does 'alā' add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q23/p1", "position": "It announces and intensifies the gravity of the condemnation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares Prophetic calls to convey and witness; Nasafī and Biqāʿī emphasize severity."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q24", "question": "What is condemned by 'evil is what they bear'?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing blame points to the evil burden itself or its recompense.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q24/p1", "position": "Their vile burden of sins or evil deeds.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Qatāda gloss the act as what they do; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it a wretched load. Zamakhsharī compares 7:177; Rāzī points to 4:22; Biqāʿī says the rebuke gathers its many defects and unbearable weight."}, {"id": "6:31/q24/p2", "position": "The punishment they suffer as recompense for evil deeds.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī records this second sense."}]}
{"id": "6:31/q25", "question": "How can 'sāʾa mā yazirūn' be parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether sāʾa functions as an ordinary verb, exclamation, or biʾsa-like blame.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q25/p1", "position": "A plain transitive past verb with mā as subject and an omitted object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites a poem; Samīn says mā may be relative, verbal or indefinite and notes the Shaykh will not fix the poem to a single parse. {"id": "6:31/q26", "question": "What do the burdens teach about the deniers' two losses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q26/p1", "position": "They failed to gain the reward they could have prepared for, while earning punishment through sins.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī pairs regret for omitted provision with burdens of committed wrong; Bursevī contrasts absent good deeds and physically borne sins; Elmalılı pairs loss of reward with enormous punishment."}]}

 the self itself.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q27/p1", "position": "The veiled deny meeting the Real; minor resurrection exposes neglected work and attachments embedded in the soul.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says bodily love, sin and sensory habits become the burdens that obstruct aims and torment the self."}, {"id": "6:31/q27/p2", "position": "The self and its very existence are the chief burden; repentance and effacement free the seeker by God's aid.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites Ḥāfiẓ against self-regard, a saying that the self cannot escape itself, and Tirmidhī on remembrance softening the heart while ego hardens it. {"id": "6:31/q29", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the pictured encounter is tied to universal resurrection or each death.", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q29/p1", "position": "It completes the portrait of people claiming worldly life alone, showing the afterlife loss their denial entails.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the opening a fresh calamity report; Ibn ʿĀshūr says explicit naming makes their fate an independent statement; Ṭabāṭabāʾī links resurrection, gathering, the Hereafter and meeting God. {"id": "6:31/q30", "question": "What general pattern of human loss does the verse illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q30/p1", "position": "Wrong paths defeat the goals for which the created order provides proper causes; apparent unjust gain ends in loss.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares trying to sustain life without eating and digestion. {"id": "6:31/q32", "question": "What is the clause structure around 'when they said'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q32/p1", "position": "'They said' answers the conditional 'when'.", "reasons": "Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr make the cry the apodosis; al-Ālūsī says the conditional is answered by 'O our remorse'."}]}

{"id": "6:31/q35", "question": "What rhetorical effect links 'awzārahum' and 'yazirūn'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:31/q35/p1", "position": "The ending yazirūn echoes awzārahum through paronomasia.", "reasons": "Burhān identifies the echo as paronomasia."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q01", "question": "What prompted the prohibition on expelling the worshippers?", "turns_on": "Which proposal the reports describe, and whether later Medinan incidents are causes or applications of a Meccan verse.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q01/p1", "position": "Quraysh or other Meccan notables demanded removal of poor believers from the Prophet's company as a condition of meeting or following him.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud, Qatada and many later transmitters name Suhayb, Ammar, Bilal, Khabbab and other poor followers; chiefs scorned their low status, dress or alleged dependence. Accounts vary on names, whether the Prophet refused, considered separate times, or a written pledge was begun. Ibn al-Anbari, Razi and Qurtubi say the Prophet hoped to win converts, not disparage believers. Reports of Sa'd put six companions there; lists differ. Khabbab also describes morning and evening teaching of Qur'an, religion and the afterlife. Ibn Zayd adds a man ashamed to be seen with Salman and Bilal, after which the Prophet was told to greet them with mercy; Baghawi transmits Mujahid's naming of Bilal and Ibn Umm Abd. Ibn Ishaq, as reported by Ibn Hisham, names Abu Fakihah Yasar alongside Khabbab, Ammar and Suhayb, and says Quraysh mocked the poor as unworthy of receiving guidance first; he connects the response to 6:52–54. Saʿd's report in Ibn Mājah names himself, Ibn Masʿūd, Suhayb, ʿAmmār, al-Miqdād and Bilāl as the six believers Quraysh wanted expelled; his report in Muslim explicitly names himself, Ibn Masʿūd and Bilāl among six."}, {"id": "6:52/q01/p2", "position": "Al-Aqra ibn Habis and Uyayna ibn Hisn requested an exclusive audience away from poor companions, sometimes before visiting Arab delegations; Gabriel's revelation interrupted a proposed written agreement.", "reasons": "Khabbab and Salman transmit this version. Accounts describe their embarrassment at wool clothes or slaves, the Prophet dropping or tearing the page, recalling the believers, sitting knee to knee, and staying until they rose; 18:28 follows in some accounts. Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur question its use as a Meccan revelation occasion because these men appeared in Medina; Ibn Ashur allows a later analogous request. Khabbab's report in Ibn Majah says Gabriel revealed 6:52 when al-Aqra and Uyayna sought private access and dismissal of the poor; it also links 6:53–54 and 18:28 to their favor and continued companionship."}, {"id": "6:52/q01/p3", "position": "The nobles requested that poor worshippers move behind them in the prayer rows, rather than leave the Prophet's gathering.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's report makes precedence in prayer the dispute; Tabari expressly contrasts this with expulsion from the gathering. Reports differ about whether nobles promised belief."}, {"id": "6:52/q01/p4", "position": "Abu Talib was approached by nobles, or himself proposed dismissing poor followers, and Umar suggested trying the request before revelation.", "reasons": "Muqatil attributes the suggestion to Abu Talib; Ikrima's account has Banu Abd Manaf petition him. Several reports say Umar apologized after the verse; names of freedmen and allies vary. Baydawi adds Umar's temporary suggestion and the arrival of Ali and a document just before revelation."}, {"id": "6:52/q01/p5", "position": "The report about al-Aqra and Uyayna is chronologically doubtful as the verse is Meccan, though a similar incident may have happened later.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir note those men became known after the Hijra; Ibn Ashur says the original verse could later answer an analogous request. Tabataba'i treats the similar stories as applications, citing the sura's single Meccan descent and unreliable occasion reports; Kuranyolu records commentators' like objection and retains the universal lesson."}, {"id": "6:52/q01/p6", "position": "A proposal to expel the Companions of the Suffa occasioned the verse.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i rejects it as a specific occasion: the sura was revealed in Mecca before the Hijra."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q02", "question": "What does ṭard mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q02/p1", "position": "It means to drive away or exclude, with a humiliating or disparaging force.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives banishment and expulsion; Abu Hayyan adds humiliation and related Arabic usage; Islahi says the harsh verb fits Quraysh's proposed contempt."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q03", "question": "Who are the people whom the Prophet must not drive away?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is limited to the original companions or its wording applies to other believers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q03/p1", "position": "The poor Muslim believers in the Prophet's company.", "reasons": "Mujahid names Bilal and Ibn Umm Abd, with one account saying Ibn Umm Ma'bad or Ibn Umm Maktum; other reports name Salman, Khabbab, Suhayb, Ammar, Ibn Masud, Sa'd, al-Miqdad, freedmen and allies. {"id": "6:52/q04", "question": "What does calling upon their Lord morning and evening denote?", "turns_on": "Whether الدعاء names prescribed prayer, particular prayers, remembrance, Quran, supplication, or comprehensive worship.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q04/p1", "position": "The prescribed prayers, sometimes all five.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ibrahim, Mujahid, Hasan, Qatada, and others say obligatory prayer; some specify congregation. A minority identifies dawn and afternoon specifically; Muqatil and Hasan describe two Meccan daily prayers before five were prescribed; Amr ibn Shuaib identifies the evening as isha. These time-specific details remain distinct in the following positions."}, {"id": "6:52/q04/p2", "position": "Specifically the dawn and afternoon prayers.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Abbas identify the two times. Mujahid sought a post-dawn remembrance gathering, but Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib rejected using this verse for storytellers."}, {"id": "6:52/q04/p6", "position": "Quran recitation, learning or honoring the Quran.", "reasons": "Abu Ja'far describes the Prophet teaching them and their reciting for God's face; Khabbab's report adds instruction in Paradise, Hell, death and resurrection."}, {"id": "6:52/q04/p7", "position": "Worship in a comprehensive sense, including prayer, remembrance, praise, and required and voluntary acts.", "reasons": "Tabari declines to narrow الدعاء: 40:60 calls worship supplication; al-Dahhak cites 40:43.
